items.title: The Patch Fear Trap: Why We Still Fear the Fix More Than the Exploit in 2026
items.summary: W arning : this blog is another experiment. The idea for a blog came from a repeat conversation I had many, many times over the years. The content is researched, debated, refined, “hardened” by a Gemini skill I created (using Gemini 4 Argon). Then Claude Fable 5.2 performed a peer review, and refined the text. Then Gemini 4 Neon looked at it and lamented “Claude staccato” style and rewrote in what it considers “Anton voice.” And then I edited it, and cut out some iffy stats AIs shoved in. Let me know if this sucks, and I will stop. Promise! Earlier this year, I kicked off my Patch Sound Barrier series by arguing that AI-driven exploit development is accelerating while legacy remediation speed is stuck with organizational “physical” limits. In Part 2 and in the 15-minute patch post , we looked at the machinery needed to remediate at a somewhat similar rate. Yet when I talk to security and IT leaders in late 2026, we keep hitting a stubborn human reality: people delay patches because they fear the patch breaking production more than the exploit . And, yes, recent incidents like the now-notorious FAA router disruption remind everyone that outages frequently happen during routine updates. In essence, they are not truly wrong. “Routine” (ha!) maintenance still triggers massive operational headaches across sectors: classified networks dropping offline, consumer platforms failing post-update, and officials reassuring the public that outages were “just routine updates” rather than cyberattacks. That is the point — routine updates are scary as hell to some people and thus those people believe they have good reasons for not remediating security flaws. Meanwhile, the exploit clock has gone negative. Mandiant’s M-Trends 2026 puts mean time-to-exploit at negative seven days — exploitation begins (in some cases!) before the vendor fix arrives. (I remember hearing “patch management is a solved problem ” back in 2006. It wasn’t.) The short takeaway: you cannot cure patch fear by yelling louder about AI exploits and threat actors. ”OMG CVSS 10 WE ARE ALL GONNA DIE” will not change the mind of a CIO who just spoke with a peer whose patch went bad a week before. To the admin on call, an exploit is a probabilistic rumor with shared blame, while a broken patch is an immediate outage with their name on the change ticket. “Attackers might hack us, but YOU will break production” is not cured by showing scarier threat intelligence. Gemini psychoanalyzes patch fears What may help? Patch fear is rational, not a culture problem. How rational? Think about fear of snakes vs. fear of flying: one is a rational reaction to an immediate physical threat in front of you; the other is an irrational phobia of a statistically safe system. So in 2026, is a security patch a plane or a snake? Snake vs plane Security teams often treat patch hesitation as a lack of “security culture” — or like a fear of flying that can be cured with more threat intel slides. It isn’t. To the sysadmin holding the pager, an untested Tuesday patch on a fragile server is a rattlesnake on the trail. It is a rational response to asymmetrical personal risk. Here is how the same vulnerability ticket looks from the two sides of the building: Table of fears Until recently, I assumed this table is very past looking, but it is definitely the present for many. Still, nobody gets fired for waiting for the change window. People do get fired for taking down production at 2 PM. As long as both statements are true, lectures about scanner queues are just noise. So yes, in 2026, admins who distrust brand-new updates have real evidence on their side. And here is the uncomfortable 2026 twist: AI didn’t just speed up the exploit clock; it degraded vendor patch quality too. Under pressure to beat negative time-to-exploit, vendors are shipping rushed point fixes while attackers point LLMs at patch diffs the hour they drop to find bypasses. According to Terra Security’s late-2026 study of published CVEs and advisories, the share of security fixes failing or requiring a follow-up patch within 90 days jumped 11.5x in 2026 (from 0.2% to 2.3%) — and bugs with bypassed fixes were 4x more likely to land on CISA’s KEV list. Do the compounding math (0.977¹⁰⁰): if you push 100 distinct updates a quarter, a 2.3% per-patch failure rate gives you a 90.25% quarterly certainty of stepping on at least one vendor-supplied landmine. Waiting 72 hours so you aren’t the vendor’s unpaid crash-test dummy isn’t laziness then. Soaking a patch in canary deployment makes sense, but waiting is only valid if: You are mitigated while you wait. Leaving exposed assets unmitigated for 14 days isn’t caution — it’s unmanaged risk today. [I am working on a general purpose mitigation framework to be revealed soon] You actively test in canaries. Passive waiting relies on others to find bugs. Your canary rings are the only test suite that matters for your stack. Rule of thumb: wait on the patch binary if you must, but never leave the risk unmitigated. Every decision to delay a patch must come with an associated mitigation decision that is right now. How to change: make patching boring instead of preaching courage Don’t demand bravery from admins. Make patching boring, reversible, and career-safe. In my maturity post , I separated time cost from learning cost. Patch fear is unpaid learning cost. Here is how to address it: Shrink the unit of change. Monolithic “pet” servers breed fear. With immutable infrastructure, spin up patched containers, divert 5% of traffic, monitor telemetry, and flip over. Fast rollback eliminates deployment anxiety. This does not help with your 1987 enterprise database, however. Rehearse rollback. Teams fear deployment because rollback procedures are untested. If reverting an update is a single rehearsed action, bad vendor updates cause minor canary blips instead of emergency war rooms. Align metrics with error budgets. Stop measuring IT purely on uptime and Security purely on resolved CVEs. Adopt SRE-style error budgets where both teams co-own release currency and change-failure budgets. Ok, many of you will read the above 3 point and this “you Anton are such a PhD” here. A fair point, these are a bit theoretical, but to break out of a current pit we do need new theories too. Not just one more of “get the slaves to work faster” slogans. Patch faster, I mean :-) The lean team reality: two clocks instead of one But yes, on a more serious note : “Anton, we can’t rewrite our core monolith into immutable microservices by next quarter,” CISOs tell me. Fair! If you are stuck with fragile legacy systems, forcing 24-hour in-place patching may cause the very outage you fear. Instead, separate risk reduction from binary replacement and run two clocks: The Mitigation Clock (Fast): When touching the host server is high-risk, sever the attack path externally within hours using identity-aware proxies, micro-segmentation, host memory shielding, or WAF virtual patching. Note: a 15-minute mitigation clock that requires a two-hour emergency CAB meeting does not exist — pre-assign standing authority to pull the mitigation switch before the advisory drops. The Patch Clock (Measured): Deploy binary fixes through deployment rings at a pace supported by testing and rollback capabilities. Then tier it. Internet-exposed or known-exploited flaws get a verified mitigation within 24 hours and the patch as fast as the rings permit. Internal, segmented and well-monitored systems can let a patch soak for 7 to 14 days on a canary ring. Word of caution: not all mitigations survive a 14-day soak window. Payload-filtering virtual patches (WAF and IPS regexes) are blocklists that secretly relied on lazy attackers — against LLM-mutated exploits, they only buy hours. To buy days or weeks for your Patch Clock, favor structural mitigations (cutting network reachability, gating by identity, or disabling the vulnerable feature) that hold even when the payload mutates. Finally, track “ mitigation debt ”: set hard expiration dates and strip out temporary blocks once the patch lands, or “mitigated” will decay into permanent rule bloat and silent risk acceptance. Potentially useful actions based on this Five plays, after you stop scolding your sysadmins for caring about uptime: Calculate your internal patch failure rate. Measure how many security updates caused outages, rollbacks, or emergency re-patching over the past four quarters so your change-control debates run on your own telemetry, not folklore. Run a “Rollback Stopwatch Drill.” Pick a Tier-1 application and time how long it actually takes to revert a bad update in staging. If the answer is “restore from backup over six hours,” spend your engineering budget on one-click rollback before demanding faster patch SLAs. Split your vulnerability SLA into a Mitigation Clock and a Patch Clock. Require a verified compensating control within 24 hours for internet-exposed or actively exploited flaws — with pre-approved standing authority to deploy it — so binary fixes can move safely through canary rings. Re-verify patches for critical vulnerabilities (and retire mitigation debt). Continuously monitor KEV fixes post-deployment to catch the 2.3% of vendor patches that break or get bypassed within 90 days, and strip out temporary WAF or firewall blocks once a verified patch holds. Fix the blame physics with a shared change-failure budget. Agree in writing between Security and Infrastructure that a rehearsed, fast-rolled-back patch hiccup inside a canary ring is a celebrated pipeline catch, not a career-limiting outage. So, will we ever fear the exploit more than the patch? No! But honestly, we shouldn’t want operations teams to stop fearing production outages. An engineering org that doesn’t care if a Tuesday afternoon update takes down the hospital, the factory floor, or the billing gateway is a dangerous org. The goal in 2026 isn’t to breed fearless sysadmins who slap rushed vendor fixes onto fragile servers and pray. The goal is to build the rollback harnesses, canary rings, and structural mitigations so that fixing — or isolating — a flaw requires zero bravery at all. To the sysadmin holding the pager, an untested Tuesday patch on a fragile server is a rattlesnake on the trail. It is a rational response to asymmetrical personal risk.

items.title: Weekly Update 531: Optimizely. Script Dependencies & Third Parties
items.summary: "You can't outsource accountability". But it feels like that's what's happening when a disclosure notice refers to "an incident being at a third party", as though somehow that makes it better. It feels like the intent is to deflect responsibility , but ultimately, accountability remains with the party we entrusted our data to in the first place. It's also ultimately them who needs to decide whether to disclose the incident, so in the case of Optimizely this week, even though it's clearly their fault, it's up to the likes of Norwegian Airlines to decide whether they're contacting impacted individuals. And then, in their case, they haven't named the third party anyway! Strange times, I reckon.

items.title: OpenRouter Users’ Private AI Chats Possibly Exposed Via Compromised Third-Party Providers
items.summary: OpenRouter has removed three AI hosting providers and revoked Zero Data Retention eligibility for 125 endpoints after researchers found evidence that some providers had been compromised or had failed to follow their data policies. In its November 22 incident notice , OpenRouter said it notified all potentially affected customers. The findings did not show a breach of OpenRouter itself, and the company did not say how many users or conversations may have been exposed. OpenRouter AI Chat Leaks OpenRouter gives customers a single API for accessing AI models hosted by different providers. But the company that first receives a request may not be the only one that handles it. If a provider forwards the request to another service, that service can also see the prompt. As Cyber Security News explained in its comparison of AI privacy gateways , routing requests and keeping them confidential are separate tasks. In its research report , Dragos said it sent nearly two million test prompts between July and November 2026. The prompts contained unique links and test credentials known as canary tokens. When a link was opened, or a credential was used, researchers could trace it to the original request. Dragos found evidence of compromises at three hosting providers. Some test requests were copied even though the model rejected them before processing. The researchers also saw signs that some requests marked for Zero Data Retention, a policy that says prompts and replies should not be stored, were kept or forwarded. In one case, a test link sent to a U.S. provider surfaced in a company chat in China 24 days later. What OpenRouter Users Should Check OpenRouter’s provider disclosures list notices from Novita, Phala, and Together. The company said it removed some endpoints from Zero Data Retention eligibility as a precaution, so the 125 removals do not represent 125 confirmed breaches. It is checking whether providers forward requests or replies to other companies and plans to verify endpoints before restoring their eligibility. Customers who received a notice should review what they sent through the affected provider. If prompts contained passwords or API keys, revoke or rotate them and check access logs for unusual activity. Earlier Cyber Security News reporting on exposed Clawdbot gateways showed why chat histories and credentials need to be reviewed together. For future requests, restrict sensitive workloads to approved providers and keep secrets out of prompts rather than relying on retention settings alone. OpenRouter AI Chat Leaks

If a provider forwards the request to another service, that service can also see the prompt. As Cyber Security News explained in its comparison of AI privacy gateways, routing requests and keeping them confidential are separate tasks.

In its research report, Dragos said it sent nearly two million test prompts between July and November 2026. The prompts contained unique links and test credentials known as canary tokens.

When a link was opened, or a credential was used, researchers could trace it to the original request. Dragos found evidence of compromises at three hosting providers. Some test requests were copied even though the model rejected them before processing.

The researchers also saw signs that some requests marked for Zero Data Retention, a policy that says prompts and replies should not be stored, were kept or forwarded. In one case, a test link sent to a U.S. provider surfaced in a company chat in China 24 days later.

What OpenRouter Users Should Check

Earlier Cyber Security News reporting on exposed Clawdbot gateways showed why chat histories and credentials need to be reviewed together. For future requests, restrict sensitive workloads to approved providers and keep secrets out of prompts rather than relying on retention settings alone.

items.title: Hackers Could Execute Commands on WordPress, Email and Print Servers Through Upload2Shell Flaw
items.summary: A flaw in Ghostscript let researchers run commands on WordPress, Roundcube webmail, and Linux print servers through routine file processing. The vulnerability, dubbed Upload2Shell and tracked as CVE-2026-125396, affects upstream Ghostscript releases before 10.08.0. It sits in the software’s Type 1 font loader, but the affected servers did not need to expose Ghostscript directly. Their own preview, thumbnail, and print features delivered files to it. The CVE record gives the flaw a CVSS 4.0 score of 8.5 and lists a local attack vector. That describes the flaw at the interpreter level, not how a document arrives there. In research published on November 17, Paulos Yibelo and pwn.ai showed that network-facing services could pass remotely supplied files to the vulnerable code. The report describes research demonstrations, not confirmed attacks in the wild. Upload2Shell Bypassed Ghostscript’s Sandbox Ghostscript renders PDFs and PostScript documents. PostScript is a programming language for describing pages, so rendering a file means running instructions from it. Ghostscript’s -dSAFER mode is meant to limit what those instructions can access. Upload2Shell undermined those limits through a use-after-free, a memory flaw in which software keeps a reference to data after releasing the memory that held it. The font loader failed to check the type of data it received before an operation that could raise an error. That error exposed a protected write that document code was not supposed to control. Researchers used the resulting memory flaw to alter Ghostscript’s security checks while -dSAFER was still enabled. The test commands ran with the renderer’s permissions, not automatically as root. As Cyber Security News reported in its coverage of a separate Ghostscript PDF flaw , those permissions help determine what an attacker can reach after gaining code execution. WordPress, Roundcube and CUPS were Exposed On WordPress, the researchers reached Ghostscript through the media preview process on a site using Imagick and ImageMagick. The WordPress advisory tracks the core upload issue separately as CVE-2026-65640. It requires media upload privileges, which Authors and higher roles have by default. As covered in our WordPress Imagick vulnerability report , WordPress fixed that route in 7.0.4 and backported the fix, including to 6.9.7. The researchers also found that certain public upload features in Forminator and Essential Addons for Elementor reached the renderer without a login in the configurations tested. On Roundcube 1.7.2, the sender needed no webmail account. The recipient had to view the message, but did not have to click or download the attachment. Roundcube’s server generated a thumbnail and passed the attachment through ImageMagick to Ghostscript. The test depended on an ImageMagick policy that allowed the handoff. The command ran as www-data , the web service account, rather than on the recipient’s device. The print server required no action from a recipient. On Debian 13, a shared CUPS queue accepted network print jobs without credentials and sent the test document to Ghostscript for conversion. The researchers confirmed command execution by writing a marker file as lp , the print service account. Requiring authentication blocked anonymous submission in the test, but did not repair the underlying flaw. These were three ways to reach the same vulnerable renderer, not three separate flaws in Ghostscript. Artifex fixed the underlying flaw in Ghostscript 10.08.0. Linux distributions can apply the same fix to an older release, so the upstream version number alone is not enough to judge exposure. Debian 13, for example, first shipped the fix in 10.05.1~dfsg-1+deb13u2 . Administrators should check their vendor’s package status for CVE-2026-125396 and verify the copy used by each service. Updating the host does not replace Ghostscript inside an existing container or application bundle. WordPress operators should apply both the core and renderer updates and review public forms that send uploads into the Media Library. If patching must wait, suspend automatic previews for untrusted files where practical. On print servers, require authentication for shared queues and restrict network access to them. Keep renderers isolated and give their service accounts only the access they need. The key check comes after a file is accepted. Storing a file did not start Ghostscript in the researchers’ tests. Rendering it did. Trace the worker that actually makes the preview, thumbnail or print output, then verify that worker uses the patched package. It sits in the software’s Type 1 font loader, but the affected servers did not need to expose Ghostscript directly. Their own preview, thumbnail, and print features delivered files to it.

The CVE record gives the flaw a CVSS 4.0 score of 8.5 and lists a local attack vector. That describes the flaw at the interpreter level, not how a document arrives there.

In research published on November 17, Paulos Yibelo and pwn.ai showed that network-facing services could pass remotely supplied files to the vulnerable code. The report describes research demonstrations, not confirmed attacks in the wild.

Upload2Shell Bypassed Ghostscript’s Sandbox

Ghostscript renders PDFs and PostScript documents. PostScript is a programming language for describing pages, so rendering a file means running instructions from it.

Ghostscript’s -dSAFER mode is meant to limit what those instructions can access. Upload2Shell undermined those limits through a use-after-free, a memory flaw in which software keeps a reference to data after releasing the memory that held it.

The font loader failed to check the type of data it received before an operation that could raise an error. That error exposed a protected write that document code was not supposed to control.

Researchers used the resulting memory flaw to alter Ghostscript’s security checks while -dSAFER was still enabled. The test commands ran with the renderer’s permissions, not automatically as root. As Cyber Security News reported in its coverage of a separate Ghostscript PDF flaw, those permissions help determine what an attacker can reach after gaining code execution.

WordPress, Roundcube and CUPS were Exposed

On WordPress, the researchers reached Ghostscript through the media preview process on a site using Imagick and ImageMagick. The WordPress advisory tracks the core upload issue separately as CVE-2026-65640. It requires media upload privileges, which Authors and higher roles have by default.

As covered in our WordPress Imagick vulnerability report, WordPress fixed that route in 7.0.4 and backported the fix, including to 6.9.7. The researchers also found that certain public upload features in Forminator and Essential Addons for Elementor reached the renderer without a login in the configurations tested.

On Roundcube 1.7.2, the sender needed no webmail account. The recipient had to view the message, but did not have to click or download the attachment. Roundcube’s server generated a thumbnail and passed the attachment through ImageMagick to Ghostscript. The test depended on an ImageMagick policy that allowed the handoff. The command ran as www-data, the web service account, rather than on the recipient’s device.

The print server required no action from a recipient. On Debian 13, a shared CUPS queue accepted network print jobs without credentials and sent the test document to Ghostscript for conversion. The researchers confirmed command execution by writing a marker file as lp, the print service account.

Requiring authentication blocked anonymous submission in the test, but did not repair the underlying flaw. These were three ways to reach the same vulnerable renderer, not three separate flaws in Ghostscript.

Artifex fixed the underlying flaw in Ghostscript 10.08.0. Linux distributions can apply the same fix to an older release, so the upstream version number alone is not enough to judge exposure. Debian 13, for example, first shipped the fix in 10.05.1~dfsg-1+deb13u2.

Administrators should check their vendor’s package status for CVE-2026-125396 and verify the copy used by each service. Updating the host does not replace Ghostscript inside an existing container or application bundle.

WordPress operators should apply both the core and renderer updates and review public forms that send uploads into the Media Library. If patching must wait, suspend automatic previews for untrusted files where practical.

On print servers, require authentication for shared queues and restrict network access to them. Keep renderers isolated and give their service accounts only the access they need.

The key check comes after a file is accepted. Storing a file did not start Ghostscript in the researchers’ tests. Rendering it did. Trace the worker that actually makes the preview, thumbnail or print output, then verify that worker uses the patched package.

items.title: Hackers Exploit Microsoft Entra Connect Health Flaw to Access Admin Emails and Organization Data
items.summary: Attackers exploited a flaw in Microsoft Entra Connect Health to read administrator and technical contact email addresses, along with configuration data from affected organizations. A Microsoft customer notice shared on Reddit describes read-only access to those records, not access to inboxes or email messages. Microsoft fixed the flaw in its cloud service on November 19, 2026, and said customers do not need to install a patch. Microsoft said the vulnerability was introduced on July 23 and detected on November 9. Investigators reviewed service logs for unauthorized requests and concluded on November 20 that attackers had read tenant data. The flaw could also have allowed changes to monitoring settings, but Microsoft found none. The notice does not say when the unauthorized access began, who was behind it, or how many organizations were affected. Entra Connect Health Flaw Exposed Microsoft Entra Connect Health lets IT teams view alerts, performance data, and directory sync errors for identity systems running on their own servers. The flaw was in the cloud monitoring service’s API. Unlike a separate Entra ID flaw involving Global Administrator privileges , this incident involved confirmed reads of tenant records, with no reported takeover of administrator accounts through the flaw. The records included each affected tenant’s ID, display name, initial domain, country code, regional scope, and Entra license tier. They also showed whether directory sync was enabled, when it last ran, and whether the organization had set up Connect Health. The API still returned an expired certificate once used to register monitoring agents with an internal Microsoft service shut down in late 2024. Microsoft said the flaw did not expose passwords, password hashes, sign-in tokens, valid cryptographic keys, Azure subscription details, or details about how local Active Directory servers were arranged. The cloud fix stopped further access through the flaw, but it cannot take back the contact details already exposed. Knowing who administers a tenant and which domain it uses could make a fake support message more convincing. Previous Microsoft 365 phishing campaigns show why unexpected sign-in requests deserve scrutiny. The notice did not report any phishing linked to this incident. Microsoft advised organizations to alert their IT and security teams, confirm their technical contact details, and require phishing-resistant multifactor authentication for privileged accounts. Where available, teams should use Privileged Identity Management to grant admin access only when needed. They should also check Connect Health settings and review Entra audit and sign-in logs and Azure Activity Logs for unexpected changes or unusual administrator activity. Administrators should open the Azure portal directly and check the security advisory in Azure Service Health to confirm whether it lists their tenant. The notice also points to Microsoft’s read-only GetTenant PowerShell script, which shows the types of records the API could have returned. It reports current values, so it cannot reconstruct what attackers saw or tell an organization which specific records were read. What Are Leading Organizations Doing About AI and Cyber Risks?
